title: Rumour: LEGO Queen Mary 2 could be next in line for the ocean liner treatment
summary: A social media leak suggests LEGO is working on a Queen Mary 2 set for 2027 or 2028, following on from the hugely popular Titanic model - but fans are hoping it won't be built fully to scale.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
A rumour, credited to leaker Carterbricks04, claims the LEGO Group is developing a model of the RMS Queen Mary 2 for a possible 2027 or 2028 release. Cunard's flagship liner has been sailing since 2004 and is still in active service today.

No piece count, price or official confirmation has been shared, and LEGO has made no announcement about this set. This follows the release of 10294 Titanic, currently the brand's most recent large-scale ocean liner build, which contains 9,090 pieces and sells for £589.99.

The Queen Mary 2 is roughly three times the physical size of the Titanic, since the century-old original was considerably smaller than today's ocean liners. If a future LEGO model matched that scale, it could theoretically require over 27,000 pieces - a huge jump from Titanic's already substantial build.

## Why it matters
Ocean liner sets like Titanic have proven popular with adult builders and collectors, so a follow-up model would likely generate plenty of interest. However, a set scaled up to match the real-world size difference could become extremely expensive and difficult to display, so many fans will be hoping for a more manageable piece count similar to or smaller than Titanic's.

## What to watch next
This is currently just a rumour, and Brick Fanatics itself has urged fans to treat it with caution until LEGO makes anything official. Keep an eye out for any leaked images, set numbers or an official reveal before getting too excited.

title: LEGO Fans Build a Samurai-Inspired Citadel for Summer Joust 2026
summary: A trio of builders teamed up for a striking Japanese-inspired castle collaboration as part of the Summer Joust 2026 fan contest, blending coastal defences, snowy monasteries and an ornate citadel.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
The Summer Joust 2026 fan-run LEGO Castle building contest has wrapped up, and one of its standout entries is a three-part collaborative build themed around "Guarding the Realm". Builders Simulterious, Vertaro and Oshi Builds each created a section of a fictional daimyo's domain.

Simulterious built Ryūshin Citadel, featuring detailed half-timbered walls, tiled roofs and a bonsai-style elevated display base. Vertaro contributed Taihō Harbor, a coastal defence scene with dragon-head cannons, a hwacha, and clever sand-texture transitions using offset SNOT (studs-not-on-top) techniques. Oshi Builds rounded things out with Gyōgaku Monastery, a snowy mountaintop scene with icy stonework and layered terrain building.

This is a fan community showcase covered by The Brothers Brick, not an official LEGO Group product or announcement.

Collaborative fan builds like this are a great source of inspiration for anyone into castle, historical or Japanese-themed MOCs (My Own Creations). title: Fan builder shares how he created a huge Wild West LEGO diorama

bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
The Brothers Brick has published a guest feature from builder Evan Crouch, known online as evanceltlego, detailing how he created a large Wild West-themed LEGO railroad diorama for the Rocky Mountain Train Show in Colorado.

According to the piece, Crouch wanted a mostly tiled layout with only a few studs visible, and aimed to capture the banded rock layers seen in nearby Utah's mountain buttes. He settled on a big 7x5 baseplate layout (35 baseplates in total, working out to 224 x 160 studs) sized to fit R72 train track, designed so local LUG members could each add their own sections to build a huge collaborative display.

He planned the project using Google Sheets to map out the layout and Studio software to test colour combinations, eventually settling on a western-inspired palette including tan, warm tan, dark tan, medium nougat, dark red, dark orange, bright light yellow, bright light orange, sand blue and reddish brown. Crouch created a 'strata map' to keep the layered rock colours consistent across different builders' sections, favouring cheaper, easier-to-source colours for the bulk of the terrain.

Sourcing the huge number of curved slopes and tiles needed took several months, using BrickLink and LEGO's online Pick A Brick service, including hunting down newer elements like warm tan pieces and printed tan tiles from recent sets.

## Why it matters
This is a great example of how much planning goes into a large-scale collaborative LEGO display, from colour theory and part-sourcing to coordinating with other builders. It's a useful read for anyone in the UK brick-building community thinking about tackling their own big diorama or joining a local LUG collaboration, especially around sourcing techniques, tiling large areas, and using tools like Studio and BrickLink to plan ahead.
